newsitem.title: russia: Yeltsin said better, opponents ease pressure.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin said better, opponents ease pressure.

text.p: The Kremlin said on Thursday that Russian President Boris Yeltsin has made progress in fighting off his pneumonia and his communist opponents eased the pressure on him to resign.
A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin's health "stabilised significantly" on Thursday, his eighth day in hospital.
"An X-ray has shown progress in curing the pneumonia," the spokesman told Reuters, reading from a prepared statement.
It was the latest in a series of optimistic reports from the Kremlin, which is keen to show that Yeltsin is fit to rule Russia two months after he had surgery to stengthen his heart.
"Today the president worked with documents for two hours, paying special attention to preparing a state of the nation address to the federal assembly," the spokesman said.
The report, an annual tradition, is due in February.
But a new opinion poll brought bad news for Yeltsin, suggesting fewer than one in four Russians trusted him while more than half trusted his bitter foe Alexander Lebed.
Yeltsin's chief doctor said on Wednesday his condition was improving but he would have to spend the rest of the week in the elite Moscow hospital where he was taken on January 8.
He said Yeltsin's disease was "treacherous" and that he should rest as much as possible to avoid complications.

Opposition leaders say the 65-year-old president, who has not appeared publicly since being taken to hospital, is not well enough to rule. One has proposed a motion for the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, to discuss trying to oust him.

On Thursday, the Duma's communist speaker said parliament should drop the motion and the man behind it, the head of the Duma Security Committee Viktor Ilyukhin, told Interfax news agency it would not come up for discussion on Friday as planned.

Gennady Seleznyov, speaker of the lower house, poured cold water on the motion after Duma experts said it could have no legal basis. "I think the issue should be removed (from the agenda)," Seleznyov said.
Ilyukhin said deputies wanted more time to consider it and that the discussion would be postponed until January 22.
Yeltsin's last significant working meeting before he fell ill was on working out Russia's response to NATO's expansion plans. Moscow says the move will threaten its security.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said in Vienna on Thursday that he wanted to have talks on relations with Russia "on target" by July, when invitations are due to go out to the first of a list of former Soviet bloc states.
Solana is due to meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Moscow on Monday.

Defence Minister Igor Rodionov told reporters that Russia remained firmly opposed to NATO's plans to expand eastwards but, avoiding tough statements, said Moscow did not plan to respond by creating its own new military bloc.
He made clear Yeltsin would have the final say but said: "For our part we are not going to expand and it does not seem we are going to set up any new military bloc."
Yeltsin's latest health scare has thwarted his efforts to assert himself over foreign policy as well as in tackling Russia's many domestic problems.

His ousted security adviser Alexander Lebed has led calls for Yeltsin to quit. Publication of the opinion poll, carried out by the Russian Independent Institute for Social and National Issues in late December, offered Yeltsin little encouragement.
The survey Lebed showed would be well placed to win a new presidential election if it were held immediately. It also revealed a wave of pessimism about Russia's prospects for 1997.
